display_title: Official Review of Paper1462 by Reviewer TbsM

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper considers the task of distinguishing between coherent and incoherent texts. The authors propose a new set of techniques for training models in such tasks and show a decent advantage over a previous method: UNC [1].

[1] Moon, Han Cheol, et al. "A unified neural coherence model." arXiv preprint arXiv:1909.00349 (2019).
content.main_review:
Pros:

1. Designing machine learning models that could produce coherent text is an important goal.
2. An extensive amount of experiments have been conducted.
3. A decent improvement over the previous state-of-the-art UNC model [1] is obtained.
4. The test set is sufficiently different from the training set and the model still works quite well (at least much better than the previous state-of-the-art UNC model [1]).

Cons:

1. There has not been a substantial amount of works studying the state-of-the-art UNC model [1]. Hence, it is unclear to me if the improvement over this method is a substantial contribution.
2. If the goal is to design ML models that could produce coherent text, it is unclear if training a model that could accurately distinguish between coherent and incoherent texts is necessary. For example, the ML model presented here is based on the pre-trained model XLNet [2]. Hence, XLNet is itself a model that could produce coherent texts. The two applications of the task studied in this work seem to be: essay scoring and sentence ordering. However, the contribution of this work seems to have less relevance in the other two applications stated in the introduction: language generation and summarization.
3. If we use the coherence model trained here (based on XLNet), I have concerns about whether the coherence model can unbiasedly score the coherence of the text generated by XLNet. Maybe the coherence model trained this way will not be able to find coherence errors in text generated by XLNet (or other similar models). The performance shown in LMvLM is also a little low.

[1] Moon, Han Cheol, et al. "A unified neural coherence model." arXiv preprint arXiv:1909.00349 (2019).
[2] Yang, Zhilin, et al. "Xlnet: Generalized autoregressive pretraining for language understanding." Advances in neural information processing systems 32 (2019).
content.summary_of_the_review: The work presents a decent improvement over a previous state-of-the-art approach. However, there is some concern regarding the significance of the task studied here.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1462 by Reviewer TbsM

content.title: Response to Reviewer TbsM (Part 1)
content.comment:
Thank you for your review! We are encouraged that you have acknowledged our effort in conducting extensive experiments, and recognize the improvements of our model over the previous SOTA model across several independent test sets that are different from the training dataset. We address your concerns here; we would appreciate your quick response so that we can address further concerns (if any) within the rebuttal time period.

**Are coherence models necessary?**

Coherence modeling is absolutely necessary! We have motivated the need for coherence evaluations in our introduction. Briefly, there have been claims of increasing fluency in texts produced by neural models, across different tasks such as summarization, language modeling, machine translation, and so on. Often, automatic word-overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE are used to evaluate these systems, which do not evaluate the quality of the text, only the overlap with the content in the reference text. 

Note that fluency does not equate to coherence; coherence is a discourse-level (that is, beyond the sentence-level) phenomena. Sentences in a coherent text are connected in systematic ways such that each sentence naturally follows the previous ones and leads into the following ones. A text produced by a system can therefore be fluent without being coherent. Neural models, particularly those which produce outputs one sentence at a time, often suffer from coherence issues. We therefore need coherence models in order to evaluate the quality of the texts the models produce. Our introduction section details the evolution of coherence modeling using the permuted document task starting from [1] when the task was introduced to [2], which is the SOTA model.

**Should we be using pre-trained models to evaluate other pre-trained models? The XLNet model may be biased in scoring the text produced by an XLNet model.**

Note that any model-based evaluation metric will beg this question; we will always be limited by the best pre-trained model when we build evaluation models. Further, we would like to point out that in our specific case, although **XLNet is pre-trained as a permuted language model, it is not a generative model of language and is therefore not capable of generating text.** 

In a more general context, given that coherence is a discourse-level phenomena, models are not automatically capable of producing coherent text even if they produce fluent text, and therefore need specific training to distinguish coherent and incoherent texts. We provide this training in the form of self-supervision from the permuted document task. We have now updated the results in Table 1 and Section 3.2 to make this clearer: 

| Model                 | WSJ   | SummEval | LMvLM | INSTED-CNN | INSTED-WIKI | StoryCloze |
| --------------------- | ----- | -------- | ----- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| UNC                   | 94.11 | 46.28    | 0.463 | 67.21      | 55.97       | 49.39      |
| XLNet (No FT)         | 71.70 | 54.93    | 0.421 | 59.96      | 53.45       | 51.69      |
| XLNet (Fully Trained) | 98.23 | 64.83    | 0.458 | 91.96      | 70.85       | 71.84      |

Note that the UNC model, which uses ELMo embeddings [3], significantly outperforms the XLNet model trained without fine-tuning (No FT) on the **WSJ** permuted document task. In addition, the UNC model also outperforms the XLNet (No FT) model on the **LMvLM**, **INSTED-CNN** and **INSTED-WIKI** datasets. This shows that the increased pre-training that the XLNet model received has not necessarily made it sensitive to coherence. Only when we fine-tune the XLNet representations on the permuted document task, the XLNet (Fully Trained) model outperforms the UNC model on the various downstream applications.

**Performance on LMvLM is low.**

We agree that this is the case; however, the task itself is quite hard. Note that the inter-annotator agreement of the human judgments for this dataset is 0.840 (high agreement) which indicates the upper bound for performance on this dataset. 

In addition, for the other test sets, the content is somewhat similar, while the texts have varying degrees of coherence. For example, in the **SummEval** dataset, different neural summarization systems produce summaries of the same source article. Language models, however, will produce texts with different contents for the same prompt; therefore, judging the comparative coherence of two texts with different content and coherence levels is a much harder task for the model. Humans however are capable of making this judgement, as evidenced by the high agreement of the annotators; we therefore hope that future work in this direction will improve results and get closer to human performance.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1462 by Reviewer MZes

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors point out that, though many claims have been made about improved coherence, studying coherence rigorously and in a fine-grained manned has been difficult. Yet, the saturation of reference-based metrics that do not consider coherence has made the need for such evaluations imperative. The authors review the history of coherence modeling and then proceed to describe the datasets used, the XLNet pretrained model, and two simplified versions of their model, which use margin-based and contrastive losses, respectively. Next, the motivation for better negative mining is described, followed by the "momentum encoder" that the authors propose to solve the problem of positive and negative examples becoming stale as training proceeds. Length invariance and hard negative mining are added on top of this for the final model, with results showing slightly better average results than the first two models described, but with standard deviation ranges that generally contain the mean points of the simpler models. For the analysis, the authors show the differences across certain hyperparameter values. Finally the authors test using different negative types (sentence intrusion and the permuted document task), as well as using a recently created manual linguistic probing dataset to identify what categories of coherence and incoherence their model is capable of finding, albeit using a different training set than was used for the majority of the paper.
content.main_review:
The authors do a good job motivating the ide athat coherence models are deeply necessary for understanding machine generative text and of contextualizing their work in connection to previous literature. However, given that their motivation is about using coherence evaluation for Natural Language Generation (NLG), I would have hoped to see at least some initial experiments that show how this model can be used for downstream applications. Equally good would have been a case study on using the proposed coherence model for evaluation. To be fair, the authors go slightly further than the previous literature by testing over different datasets that likely have distribution shift from the training set, but fundamentally the authors leave it implicit what should be done with coherence models.

While the single baseline is beaten by the proposed models, I have a few worries about the results.

First of all, the only baseline provided does *extremely* poorly, often worse than random! Surely if it is simply the case that all previous models do so poorly under distribution shift then more intermediate models could have been shown that do worse than the proposed model but better than random.

Second the final proposed model is significantly more complicated than the two simplified versions described in 3.2 and 3.3, but it rarely outperforms the average results of these simplified models by more than a standard deviation.

Third, it seems highly likely that much of transfer this model achieves is a result of using a pretrained model, but this is never properly addressed, e.g. by using pretrained models for baselines, trying to finetune different pretrained models, etc.

Fourth, ablations for the final model are lacking, though the exploration of different hyperparameters is enlightening and appreciated. 

The analysis is also somewhat inconsistent, i.e., for the Permuted Document Tasks only one dataset is used from the previous analysis, with a footnote that this setup "generalized better" rather than simply showing the full results.

Altogether, I feel that though the motivation of this paper is good, the results presented don't have convincing baselines, ablations, or downstream applications that showcase why the proposed model is something that should be adopted by others. The architecture+training methodology in 3.4 is certainly somewhat novel, but without being properly ablated it is hard to know how useful this novelty is.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the problem of coherence modeling is important, I do not think this paper should be accepted. The gains over the single baseline are drastic, without much analysis as to why the difference is so huge or what models might fill the space inbetween, while the complete model isn't properly ablated. Finally, the case for how the specific kind of coherence model that the authors develop can be used isn't clear. I recommend to reject this paper in its current form.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1462 by Reviewer MZes

content.title: Response to Reviewer MZes (Part 1)
content.comment:
Thank you for your review! We are glad that you think we did a good job motivating the need for our work in improving coherence models, and that you acknowledge our efforts to go further than previous work by testing on different datasets. We address your concerns here; we would appreciate your quick response so that we can address further concerns (if any) within the rebuttal time period.


**There are no experiments to show this model can be used for downstream applications.**

This is not the case! We would like to call attention to the fact that out of the 6 datasets that we present results on, 3 are in fact downstream applications:

- **SummEval** (Section 2.2) is a test set created from machine generated summaries produced by various SOTA neural summarization systems. We have used the coherence judgements from humans collected by [1] to compare our model performance. Our model is considered to be correct if it gives a higher score to the text judged by humans to be more coherent.
- **LMvLM** (Section 2.2) is a test set created from language model outputs from various GPT and CTRL models. We used the outputs produced by the language models for a given prompt to conduct a user study from which we obtained pairwise coherence judgments from humans. Similar to the **SummEval** dataset, our model is considered to be correct if it gives a higher score to the text judged by humans to be more coherent.
- **StoryCloze** (Section 2.3) is a commonsense reasoning dataset; we followed [2] in testing coherence models on this dataset as a downstream application. The last sentence in a given text may or may not be congruent with the preceding context sentences; our model is considered to be correct if it gives a higher score to the text with a congruent last sentence.

We reported the results on all 3 downstream applications throughout the paper. We also performed an in-depth analysis of the types of coherence that our model is capable of detecting in Section 4.4. **We would also like to highlight here that the model we used for the analysis is our best performing model trained on the WSJ permuted document task, which is in fact the training task/data we have used throughout the paper.** Our model does not yet match human performance, but we hope that our contributions in changing the training and testing paradigm for coherence models will encourage more research in this direction that will bridge the gap that we still have for off-the-shelf evaluations.

**UNC might be a weak baseline, and model improvements are mostly contributed by pretrained XLNet representations.**

Note that the UNC model uses ELMo [3] representations, *which are pre-trained*. We agree that the results we present may give that impression, and decided to take Reviewer faZN’s advice on presenting results of an XLNet model without fine-tuning the representations. Specifically, only the score-producing linear layer weights $\mathbf{w}$ and $b$ are trained on the pairwise ranking task. These results are now updated in Table 1 and Section 3.2. 

| Model                 | WSJ   | SummEval | LMvLM | INSTED-CNN | INSTED-WIKI | StoryCloze |
| --------------------- | ----- | -------- | ----- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| UNC                   | 94.11 | 46.28    | 0.463 | 67.21      | 55.97       | 49.39      |
| XLNet (NO FT)         | 71.70 | 54.93    | 0.421 | 59.96      | 53.45       | 51.69      |
| XLNet (Fully Trained) | 98.23 | 64.83    | 0.458 | 91.96      | 70.85       | 71.84      |


Our XLNet-Pairwise model trained without fine-tuning the representations (No FT) has some success on the **SummEval** and **StoryCloze** datasets compared to UNC, but overall the performance of this model is worse. This shows that *the UNC model is in fact a strong baseline* model despite using ELMo [3] pretrained representations. This is particularly evident from the performance on the in-task WSJ test set; we see that the UNC model performance is significantly higher (94.11%) compared to XLNet (No FT) model (71.70%). These results further emphasize the conclusions drawn by [2] and [4] which show that SOTA coherence models are designed to perform very well on the **WSJ** permuted document task but fail to generalize to other datasets and tasks. Table 6 in the Appendix (A.5) lists the results obtained by [2] and [4] on various tasks that show that the UNC model outperforms other existing coherence models on various tasks.

content.title: Response to Reviewer MZes (Part 2)
content.comment:
**Only one dataset is used for the analysis on the Permuted Document Task.**

We agree that including results from training the model on both the **INSTED** datasets would have been a better way to compare the models, and apologize for the oversight. We have now updated Table 2 and Section 4.3 to include these results:

| Training Data | Task               | WSJ   | SummEval | LMvLM | INSTED-CNN | INSTED-WIKI | StoryCloze |
| ------------- | ------------------ | ----- | -------- | ----- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| INSTED-CNN    | Sentence Intrusion | 95.48 | 57.85    | 0.502 | 97.83      | 73.52       | 71.75      |
| INSTED-CNN    | Permuted Document  | 97.03 | 66.63    | 0.483 | 92.61      | 69.88       | 68.95      |
| INSTED-WIKI   | Sentence Intrusion | 95.24 | 53.03    | 0.490 | 94.07      | 82.01       | 64.21      |
| INSTED-WIKI   | Permuted Document  | 96.89 | 64.53    | 0.491 | 84.17      | 71.35       | 69.09      |
| WSJ           | Permuted Document  | 98.23 | 64.83    | 0.458 | 91.96      | 70.85       | 71.84      |

The objective of this analysis was to determine if the sentence intrusion task generalizes better than the permuted document task, and how other datasets compare to the WSJ dataset on the permuted document task. We have now modified Section 4.3 to make this comparison clear. 

We see that training on the permuted document task on **INSTED-WIKI** leads to a drop in performance on the **INSTED-WIKI** sentence intrusion test set. The sentence-intrusion task is a hard task; our model performance is reasonable considering it is trained on a different dataset and task setting. We see that the permuted document task overall generalizes better. Additionally, the performance of our **WSJ** model on the **INSTED-CNN** and **INSTED-WIKI** datasets is comparable to the performance of the respective in-domain pairwise models, while outperforming both the other models on the **StoryCloze** dataset. Overall, the **WSJ** model generalizes well.



**Final model is complicated and improvement over its simpler version is not adequate.**

Note that the improvements that we showcase are consistent across 6 separate test sets, 5 of which are *independent test sets*, that is, the results are obtained through a model that is trained on the **WSJ** dataset using a self-supervision task that does not *directly* reflect the task of the independent test set. *In light of this, our model’s improvements are significant.* 

We would also like to draw attention to the complexity of the previous SOTA UNC [5] model, which was designed to be very good at the permuted document task at the expense of its ability to generalize to downstream applications. We have made extensive efforts to show that our model does not suffer from this issue.

Our main objective in this paper is to change the existing training and testing paradigm in coherence modeling, which previously only trained and tested pairwise models on the **WSJ** permuted document task. Our goal is to fuel further research within a new paradigm of using a larger number of negatives for training and performing extensive evaluations on downstream applications to show generalization ability. 



[1] Fabbri at al., Summeval: Re-evaluating Summarization Evaluation. TACL 2021  
[2] Pishdad et al., How Coherent Are Neural Models of Coherence? COLING 2020  
[3] Peters et al., Deep Contextualized Word Representations. NAACL 2018  
[4] Mohiuddin et al.,  Rethinking Coherence Modeling: Synthetic vs. Downstream Tasks. EACL 2021  
[5] Moon et al.,  A unified neural coherence model. EMNLP 2019

display_title: Official Review of Paper1462 by Reviewer faZN

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper discusses the problem of coherence modeling. It points out that although previous works have conducted wide research on coherence modeling, they can only perform well on the permuted document task while cannot generalize well to downstream tasks. 

In this work, the authors propose a coherence model based on contrastive learning that can generalize well and can be used off-the-shelf for other downstream applications. Based on a pretrained XLNet, the authors adopt pairwise ranking, contrastive learning and momentum encoder to enhance the performance. The authors also propose to mine harder negative samples to boost the effect of contrastive learning. Several evaluation datasets are collected from downstream tasks and the authors compare their proposed methods with the current state-of-the-art methods. Experimental results demonstrate that their methods are superior to the current SOTA models. Further analyses demonstrate that the proposed methods can generalize well to downstream applications in different settings.
content.main_review:
Pros:

1. The problem of modeling coherence for downstream applications is important and can have an extensive impact on further research and evaluations.

2. It is a natural thought to adopt contrastive learning to perform self-supervised learning on the task of coherence modeling. The proposed methods can outperform the current SOTA methods, and also they demonstrate better generalization ability on several downstream evaluation datasets.

3. The "local negative sample ranking" method is effective since mining harder negative samples is proved to be useful. The experimental results in the paper proves that the proposed "local ranking method" can reduce the search space of candidate negative samples. 
The paper is well-written and easy to understand.

Cons:

1. The SOTA baseline used in the paper, UNC, is a non-pretrained model, while the proposed methods in this paper are based on XLNet. Considering the large pretraining corpus, it is imaginable that XLNet-based methods can perform better and generalize better to downstream tasks. It is also shown in [1] that a pretrained model can overperform UNC and many other strong baselines. Given the results in Table 1, the performance gain seems to be mainly brought by incorporating XLNet as the base network while the contribution of contrastive learning seems marginal. 
    
    (a). One question I want to raise here is that I wonder how the performance will be if XLNet is evaluated on these datasets before finetuning. Such a comparison can show how much domain knowledge is contained in a un-finetuned XLNet.
    
    (b). Another alternative experiment is to apply the proposed contrastive learning objective to the SOTA baseline, UNC, and see if contrastive learning can bring improvements to it.

2. Some experimental results lack interpretation. For example, 
    
    (a). In Figure 2a, why will harder negative samples cause instability to the basic contrastive model? Is such a phenomenon observed in previous research or on other tasks? 
    
    (b). Since Table 1 and Figure 2b only compares the influence of h, how will be the results if no hard sample mining method is adopted here?

3. I am also concerned how much contribution such methods can bring to the evaluations of downstream applications. This paper mainly discusses generalizale coherence modeling. However, as shown in Table 1 and Table 2, when trained on INSTED-WIKI dataset, the performance on INSTED-WIKI is 82.01. But if trained on WSJ, the performance on INSTED-WIKI will degrade to 72.04. It seems to be a large gap. So I am concerned about whether we can regard it as a good generalization if such a gap exists. Also when we really use a model with this generalization performance to evaluate downstream tasks, how confident will the predictions be?
    
    (a). I would like to see more comparisons between the generalized results and results trained on the dataset in the same domain. This can help with understanding of how confident the model generalization ability will be. 

[1] Abhishek et al., Transformer Models for Text Coherence Assessment, Arxiv preprint
content.summary_of_the_review: This work studies a fundamental task of modeling coherence for downstream applications. The experiments can well support the claims of the advantages for the proposed methods. However, I am concerned if the improvements are mostly brought by the pretrained models. As stated in Cons 1, more experiments on a un-finetuned XLNet or adapting the proposed contrastive objective to the current SOTA model (UNC) will help to clarify this. Also, more discussions on the experimental results and more experiments on evaluating the generalization ability will help to make this work stronger.

Specifically, only the score-producing linear layer weights $\mathbf{w}$ and $b$ are trained on the pairwise ranking task. These results are now updated in Table 1 and Section 3.2. 

| **Model**                 | **WSJ**   | **SummEval** | **LMvLM** | **INSTED-CNN** | **INSTED-WIKI** | **StoryCloze** |
| --------------------- | ----- | -------- | ----- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| UNC                   | 94.11 | 46.28    | 0.463 | 67.21      | 55.97       | 49.39      |
| XLNet (No FT)         | 71.70 | 54.93    | 0.421 | 59.96      | 53.45       | 51.69      |
| XLNet (Fully Trained) | 98.23 | 64.83    | 0.458 | 91.96      | 70.85       | 71.84      |

Our XLNet-Pairwise model trained without fine-tuning the representations (No FT) has some success on the **SummEval** and **StoryCloze** datasets compared to UNC, but overall the performance of this model is worse. This shows that *the UNC model is in fact a strong baseline* model despite using ELMo [2] pretrained representations. This is particularly evident from the performance on the in-task **WSJ** test set; we see that the UNC model performance is significantly higher (94.11%) compared to XLNet (No FT) model (71.70%). These results further emphasize the conclusions drawn by [3] and [4] which show that SOTA coherence models are designed to perform very well on the **WSJ** permuted document task but fail to generalize to other datasets and tasks. Table 6 in the Appendix (A.5) lists the results obtained by [3] and [4] on various tasks that show that the UNC model outperforms other existing coherence models on various tasks.  


**Why is hard negative training unstable? Has this phenomenon been observed in previous work?**  

Yes, there is some existing work in this regard. We refer to [5], who present a summary of such cases and show that training with the hardest negatives can lead to bad local minima. This can be explained with the gradient analysis of such negatives which have a larger gradient norm [6], resulting in abrupt gradient steps. The momentum encoder can be considered as a *temporal ensemble* model consisting of exponential-moving-average versions of the base model. Due to this, the gradients from the momentum loss also help in stabilising the overall training. In other words, being a temporal ensemble of the base models, the momentum encoder has a regularizing effect, addressing this issue and leading to stable and improved results. We have now updated the paper to include a short note about this in Section 4.1.   


[1] Abhishek et al., Transformer Models for Text Coherence Assessment. Arxiv preprint  
[2] Peters et al., Deep Contextualized Word Representations. NAACL 2018  
[3] Pishdad et al., How Coherent Are Neural Models of Coherence? COLING 2020  
[4] Mohiuddin et al.,  Rethinking Coherence Modeling: Synthetic vs. Downstream Tasks. EACL 2021  
[5] Xuan et al., Hard Negative Examples Are Hard, but Useful. ECCV 2020  
[6] Xiong et al., Approximate Nearest Neighbor Negative Contrastive Learning for Dense Text Retrieval. ICLR 2021

content.title: Response to Reviewer faZN (Part 2)
content.comment:
**Is the model really generalizing? There is a large gap in performance on the INSTED-WIKI dataset.**

It seems there is a misunderstanding here. We would like to call attention to the fact that the two quoted numbers compared (82.01 and 72.04) are trained *not only on different domains but on different tasks.* The **INSTED-WIKI** task is to detect sentence-intrusion (Section 2.3). When the model is trained on the sentence-intrusion task on **INSTED-WIKI** - which means both the domain and the training task setting match - the performance is 82.01. When the model is trained on the **WSJ** permuted task (both domain and task setting do not match), the performance is 72.04. 
We agree that including results from training the model on the permuted document task on the **INSTED-WIKI** dataset would have been more illuminating about the generalization ability of the model. We have now updated Table 2 and Section 4.3 to include these results and make the objective of our comparisons clearer. 

| Training Data | Task               | WSJ   | SummEval | LMvLM | INSTED-CNN | INSTED-WIKI | StoryCloze |
| ------------- | ------------------ | ----- | -------- | ----- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| INSTED-WIKI   | Sentence Intrusion | 95.24 | 53.03    | 0.490 | 94.07      | 82.01       | 64.21      |
| INSTED-WIKI   | Permuted Document  | 96.89 | 64.53    | 0.491 | 84.17      | 71.35       | 69.09      |

We see that training on the permuted document task on **INSTED-WIKI** leads to a drop in performance on the **INSTED-WIKI** sentence intrusion test set. The sentence-intrusion task is a hard task; our model performance is reasonable considering it is trained on a different dataset and task setting. The main objective of the comparisons in Table 2 was to investigate whether the sentence intrusion task may make for better coherence self-supervision; we show that the permuted document task overall generalizes better. 
We have made two main contributions which we hope will fuel further research into coherence modeling that will bridge the gap we still have on downstream application datasets such as **LMvLM**:

- We have shown through extensive experiments that the standard pairwise ranking setting is inadequate, and that increasing the number of negatives during training improves the model performance both on the permuted document task and on downstream applications.
- We have introduced a new, rigorous evaluation paradigm by extensively testing the model on multiple test sets, including downstream applications like machine generated summaries (**SummEval**), language model outputs (**LMvLM**), and common sense reasoning (**StoryCloze**), in addition to coherence-based test sets (**WSJ, INSTED-CNN, INSTED-WIKI**).

content.main_review:
Pros:
1. The paper is simple and easy to understand, and the problem in this paper is also interesting

Questions / Cons: 
However, I do have some questions/concerns, and think there might be some way to improve the paper.

(1) In section 3.1., based on my understanding, [CLS] token is appended in every sentence in XLNet, rather than the document D. Could you help me clarify this part? Without proper pre-training, the generalization ability of the model is typically not good since the domain of the text could be significantly different. Instead the proposed method is modified from XLNet, a model trained on a very large-scale dataset, so it is not really a fair comparison. 

(3) Also for the results in table 1, "Our- Pairwise" model already outperforms UNC baseline by a large margin, though it only use the pairwise ranking loss, and it hasn't incorporated any components introduced in the paper yet. After introducing contrastive loss by using more negatives, the model's improvement seems really marginal compare with simple pairwise baseline. replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1462 by Reviewer 7WP7

content.title: Response to Reviewer 7WP7 (Part 1)
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments! We are glad that you found our work interesting, our paper simple and easy to understand, and recognized our effort in presenting our results that improve over previous SOTA while requiring less computation compared to previous work in hard negative mining. We address your concerns here; we would appreciate your quick response so that we can address further concerns (if any) within the rebuttal time period.

**The model was tested ONLY on coherent dataset, so we are not sure if the proposed objective could be transfer to other downstream tasks.**

This is not the case! We would like to call attention to the fact that out of the 6 datasets that we present results on, 3 are in fact downstream applications:

- **SummEval** (Section 2.2) is a test set created from machine generated summaries produced by various SOTA neural summarization systems. We have used the coherence judgements from humans collected by [1] to compare our model performance. Our model is considered to be correct if it gives a higher score to the text judged by humans to be more coherent.
- **LMvLM** (Section 2.2) is a test set created from language model outputs from various GPT and CTRL models. We used the outputs produced by the language models for a given prompt to conduct a user study from which we obtained pairwise coherence judgments from humans. Similar to the **SummEval** dataset, our model is considered to be correct if it gives a higher score to the text judged by humans to be more coherent.
- **StoryCloze** (Section 2.3) is a commonsense reasoning dataset; we followed [2] in testing coherence models on this dataset as a downstream application. The last sentence in a given text may or may not be congruent with the preceding context sentences; our model is considered to be correct if it gives a higher score to the text with a congruent last sentence.

We reported the results on all 3 downstream applications throughout the paper. We also performed an in-depth analysis of the types of coherence that our model is capable of detecting in Section 4.4. 

**UNC might be a weak baseline, and model improvements are mostly contributed by pretrained XLNet representations.**

Note that the UNC model uses ELMo [3] representations, *which are pre-trained*. We agree that the results we present may give that impression, and decided to take your advice on presenting results of an XLNet model without fine-tuning the representations. Specifically, only the score-producing linear layer weights $\mathbf{w}$ and $b$ are trained on the pairwise ranking task. These results are now updated in Table 1 and Section 3.2. 

| **Model**                 | **WSJ**   | **SummEval** | **LMvLM** | **INSTED-CNN** | **INSTED-WIKI** | **StoryCloze** |
| --------------------- | ----- | -------- | ----- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| UNC                   | 94.11 | 46.28    | 0.463 | 67.21      | 55.97       | 49.39      |
| XLNet (No FT)         | 71.70 | 54.93    | 0.421 | 59.96      | 53.45       | 51.69      |
| XLNet (Fully Trained) | 98.23 | 64.83    | 0.458 | 91.96      | 70.85       | 71.84      |

Our XLNet-Pairwise model trained without fine-tuning the representations (No FT) has some success on the **SummEval** and **StoryCloze** datasets compared to UNC, but overall the performance of this model is worse. This shows that *the UNC model is in fact a strong baseline* model despite using ELMo [3] pretrained representations. This is particularly evident from the performance on the in-task **WSJ** test set; we see that the UNC model performance is significantly higher (94.11%) compared to XLNet (No FT) model (71.70%). These results further emphasize the conclusions drawn by [2] and [4] which show that SOTA coherence models are designed to perform very well on the **WSJ** permuted document task but fail to generalize to other datasets and tasks. Table 6 in the Appendix (A.5) lists the results obtained by [2] and [4] on various tasks that show that the UNC model outperforms other existing coherence models on various tasks. 

**Final model improvements are not adequate.**

Note that the improvements that we showcase are consistent across 6 separate test sets, 5 of which are *independent test sets*, that is, the results are obtained through a model that is trained on the **WSJ** dataset using a self-supervision task that does not directly reflect the task of the independent test set. *In light of this, our model’s improvements are significant.* 

Our main objective in this paper is to change the existing training and testing paradigm in coherence modeling, which previously only trained and tested pairwise models on the **WSJ** permuted document task. Our goal is to fuel further research within a new paradigm of using a larger number of negatives for training and performing extensive evaluations on downstream applications to show generalization ability.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 7WP7 (Part 2)
content.comment:
**The number of negative examples (5) seems quite small, have you tried a larger number?**

Resource constraints prevent us from training with a larger number of negative samples. As we detail in Section 3.4, the solution often adopted in such circumstances is to consider other positive instances in the same training batch as negatives. This solution is not suitable for the permuted document task since the negatives are instance-specific (permutations of the positive document). 

The other solution is to use a global negative queue that is independent of the current training instance, which is the solution we adapt to our task, using a momentum encoder to enforce representation consistency.  The experiments we report use a global negative queue of size 1000.  The loss from the momentum encoded global negative queue is weighted and combined with the main contrastive loss to ensure that the primary supervision still comes from the instance-specific negatives. 

**[CLS] token is appended in every sentence in XLNet, rather than the document D. Could you help me clarify this part?**

The [CLS] token is a document-level representation and is therefore appended to the end of the full input document and not after every individual sentence. Typically, [SEP] tokens are used to obtain sentence-level representations; we do not use them in our model. 

**Also the notation in this part is not clear, for example, where does t in v_t come from?**

The $t$ in $v_t$ refers to the index of some token $w_t$ out of the words $w_1 \dots w_k$ in the given input. We have updated the description in Section 3.1 to clarify this. 

**Is b considered as a parameter that needs to be trained (since it does not appear in $\theta$)?**

Yes, $b$ is also a parameter that is trained. We missed this, thank you for pointing it out! We have updated the description in Section 3.1 to include it.

**Table 2 uses "contrastive" as model name, which model does it refer to, "full" or "contrastive" as stated in table 1.**

Originally, it referred to the “contrastive” and not the “full” model as in Table 1. We apologize for the confusion. We have now revised Table 2 to include new results. The objective of this analysis was to determine if the sentence intrusion task generalizes better than the permuted document task, and how other datasets perform compared to the WSJ dataset on the permuted document task. We have now modified Section 4.3 to make this comparison clear.
 
In general, we show that the permuted document task generalizes better than the sentence-intrusion task. In addition, the performance of our WSJ model on the INSTED-CNN and INSTED-WIKI datasets is comparable to the performance of the respective in-domain pairwise models, while outperforming both the other models on the StoryCloze dataset. Overall, the WSJ model generalizes well.

[1] Fabbri at al., Summeval: Re-evaluating Summarization Evaluation. TACL 2021  
[2] Pishdad et al., How Coherent Are Neural Models of Coherence? COLING 2020  
[3] Peters et al., Deep Contextualized Word Representations. NAACL 2018  
[4] Mohiuddin et al.,  Rethinking Coherence Modeling: Synthetic vs. Downstream Tasks. EACL 2021
